CausalChain: Phytochemical design via AI optimization -> Specific binding to MALAT1 triple helix -> Induced conformational change in MALAT1 -> Disruption of MALAT1-EZH2 interaction -> Altered recruitment of epigenetic modifiers -> Reprogramming of chromatin states and gene expression -> Enhanced chemotherapy sensitivity
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that specifically engineered, plant-derived phytochemicals, optimized using machine learning and computational molecular dynamics, encapsulated within nuclear-targeted exosome–liposome hybrid nanoparticles, can selectively bind to the triple helix domain of MALAT1. This binding event induces a conformational change in the MALAT1 structure, thereby effectively disrupting its interaction with the epigenetic modifier EZH2. The disruption alters the subsequent recruitment of chromatin-remodeling complexes, leading to a reprogramming of the epigenetic landscape and gene expression profiles in tumor cells. Consequently, these molecular alterations result in enhanced sensitivity of cancer cells to conventional chemotherapeutic agents. This hypothesis will be tested and validated using a combination of advanced in silico simulations, high-resolution biophysical binding assays, CRISPR-mediated functional studies, and real-time imaging of nanoparticle delivery and nuclear targeting.
Abstract: We propose that next‐generation, machine‐learning–optimized, plant‐derived phytochemicals, when encapsulated within advanced nuclear‐targeted exosome–liposome hybrid nanoparticles engineered via multimodal imaging-guided assembly, can precisely bind to the triple helix region of MALAT1. This binding triggers a conformational change that disrupts MALAT1’s interaction with the epigenetic regulator EZH2, thereby altering the recruitment and activity of chromatin modifiers and reprogramming gene expression profiles in tumor cells. The epigenetic reprogramming is hypothesized to sensitize the tumor cells to conventional chemotherapy. Our approach will integrate state-of-the-art in silico molecular dynamics simulations with AI-driven drug design, high-resolution biophysical binding assays, CRISPR-based mechanistic evaluations, and live-cell imaging to optimize nanoparticle formulation, bolster nuclear delivery, and rigorously validate the therapeutic mechanism.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis retains all the key steps of the original causal chain: (1) targeted phytochemical binding to the MALAT1 triple helix, (2) induced conformational change in MALAT1, (3) disruption of the MALAT1-EZH2 interaction, (4) altered recruitment of epigenetic modifiers, and (5) reprogramming of chromatin and gene expression leading to increased chemosensitivity. However, we have enhanced its practical implementability by integrating contemporary technologies. Specifically, we now propose the use of AI and machine learning for optimizing phytochemical design, advanced nuclear-targeted exosome–liposome hybrid nanoparticles guided by multimodal imaging to ensure efficient nuclear delivery, and high-resolution real-time assays to validate each step. These modifications directly address concerns regarding specificity, delivery efficiency, and validation of the mechanistic steps in the original hypothesis.
